ru: ложиться, лечь; прилечь, полежать
separable: no object — nothing ever comes between *lie* and *down*; where and how long follow after: *lie down on the couch*, *lie down for an hour*
gloss: To put your body flat on a surface in order to rest.
examples: Go *lie down* for an hour and see if the headache passes.
She *lay down* on the couch and was asleep in a minute.
The dog had *lain down* right across the doorway.
contrast: *Lie down* is what you do yourself: *lie, lay, lain*. *Lay down* is what you do to something else: *lay, laid, laid*. So *she lay down* is last night's rest, but *she laid down the book* is a different verb. Note that *lay* is both the past of *lie* and the present of *lay* — that is where learners lose the thread.

ru: набрасываться, наброситься (на кого-л.); отчитывать, отчитать; накидываться
separable: inseparable — the person follows *into*: *light into him*, *light into the coach*; never ✗ *light him into*
gloss: To attack someone suddenly with angry words or with blows.
examples: My father *lit into* me for coming home at two in the morning.
She'll *light into* anybody who criticizes her kids.
He had *lit into* the referee before we could pull him away.
contrast: American English keeps the short past here: *lit into*, not ✗ *lighted into*. (*Lighted* survives only for lamps and candles: *a lighted window*.)

ru: притворяться, притвориться; играть в воображаемое; воображать
separable: fixed — *believe* is part of the verb and never moves; what you pretend comes after as a clause: *make believe you're asleep*
transitivity: intransitive — it takes a clause, not an object: *made believe he hadn't heard*
gloss: To pretend that something is true, especially as a game.
examples: The kids *make believe* the couch is a pirate ship.
We *made believe* we hadn't seen him come in.
She spent the whole afternoon *making believe* she was a doctor.
contrast: Two words as a verb — *they make believe* — but hyphenated as a noun or adjective: *a world of make-believe*, *a make-believe friend*.

ru: вносить, внести (деньги); отчислять, отчислить; делать взносы
separable: usually stands alone — *you pay in for forty years* — or takes the amount right after: *pay in two hundred a month*. It does split around an object: *paid the whole amount in*, *pay it in*
transitivity: both — intransitive (*we both pay in every month*), transitive (*paid in another five hundred*)
gloss: To put money into a fund, a plan, or a shared pot.
examples: Everybody in the office *pays in* ten dollars a week.
He *paid in* for thirty years and drew his first check at sixty-five.
She had *paid* the whole amount *in* before she turned fifty.
contrast: *Paid* has one *d* and no *y*: *paid in*, never ✗ *payed in*.

ru: посвящать, посвятить (в курс дела); допускать, допустить к закрытой информации
separable: separable, and usually split — the person goes in the middle: *read her in*, *read the new analyst in*; what she is told follows *on*: *read him in on the plan*
gloss: To give someone official access to information they were not allowed to have before.
examples: Only four people have been *read in* on the project.
They *read* her *in* the day she transferred.
I'll *read in* the rest of the team on Monday.
contrast: All three forms are spelled *read*, but the sound changes: present /riːd/ (REED), past and participle /rɛd/ (RED). *They read him in yesterday* rhymes with *bed*.

ru: изучать, изучить (материал); читать, почитать о чём-л.; подчитывать
separable: no object of its own — the subject follows *on* or *about*: *read up on the case*; never ✗ *read the case up*
gloss: To learn about a subject by reading as much as you can about it.
examples: *Read up* on the company before the interview.
I *read up* on Texas water law all weekend.
She's been *reading up* about adoption for months.
contrast: The spelling never changes, but the past is said /rɛd/: *I read up on it last night* rhymes with *bed*, while *I read up on it every night* rhymes with *bead*.

ru: составлять, составить (сумму); доходить до, достигать; насчитывать
separable: inseparable — the amount follows *to*: *ran to four thousand dollars*; never ✗ *ran the bill to*
gloss: To reach a particular total or size.
examples: The repair bill *ran to* almost four thousand dollars.
His report *runs to* three hundred pages.
By the time we were finished, the list had *run to* sixty names.
contrast: *Run* has a past of its own but the participle goes back to the base: *run, ran, run*. *It has ran to* is not English — *it has run to* is.

ru: бежать жаловаться (кому-л.); обращаться, обратиться за помощью
separable: inseparable — the person follows *to*: *run to her lawyer*, *run to me*; never ✗ *run me to*
gloss: To go to someone for help or sympathy instead of handling something yourself.
examples: Don't *run to* me when the landlord calls.
He *ran to* his father the second things got hard.
She's *run to* the same friend with every problem since college.

ru: понимать скрытую суть; видеть насквозь; разбираться в чём-л.
separable: inseparable — what you understand follows *into*: *see into his motives*, *see into it*; never ✗ *see his motives into*
gloss: To understand the hidden truth or the real nature of something.
examples: A good teacher can *see into* a kid's silence.
She *saw into* his motives long before the rest of us did.
Nobody has ever really *seen into* that family.
contrast: *See* changes shape twice: *see, saw, seen*. *Seen* never stands on its own — ✗ *I seen into it* is a common spoken error; write *I saw into it* or *I have seen into it*.

ru: осматривать, осмотреть (дом, помещение); обходить с осмотром
separable: inseparable — the place follows *over*: *see over the house*, *see over it*. Americans more often say *look over* or *walk through*; *see over* has a slightly formal, real-estate ring to it
gloss: To walk through a building or property and look at all of it.
examples: We drove out to *see over* the barn before making an offer.
They *saw over* three apartments in one afternoon.
The place had already been *seen over* by two other buyers.

ru: зашивать, зашить; сшивать, сшить; заштопать
separable: separable — *sew up the hem*, *sew the hem up*, *sew it up*; a pronoun has to sit in the middle, never ✗ *sew up it*
gloss: To close an opening or a tear with stitches.
examples: She *sewed up* the tear before anyone noticed.
The doctor had the cut *sewn up* in ten minutes.
Give me the jacket and I'll *sew* the pocket *up*.
contrast: *Sew* is regular in the past — *sewed up* — but irregular in the participle: *sewn up*. *Sewed* is also heard as a participle, but *sewn* is the safer written form. Do not confuse it with *sow* (to plant seed), which sounds like *cow*.

ru: обеспечивать, обеспечить (победу, сделку); улаживать, уладить окончательно
separable: separable — *sew up the deal*, *sew the deal up*, *sew it up*; the passive *it's all sewn up* is the form you hear most
gloss: To settle something completely so that the outcome is no longer in doubt.
examples: Two more states and she has the nomination *sewn up*.
They *sewed up* the contract over dinner.
Don't worry about the venue — I'll *sew* that *up* tomorrow.

ru: вылетать, вылететь; выбрасываться, выброситься (резко); метнуться
separable: no object — *his hand shot out*; the two words stay together
gloss: To move out or forward suddenly and very fast.
examples: His hand *shot out* and caught the glass before it hit the floor.
Flames *shoot out* of that pipe every time they test the burner.
A cat came *shooting out* from under the porch.
contrast: *Shoot* has one form for both past and participle: *shot* — *it shot out*, *it has shot out*. Never ✗ *shooted*.

ru: расстреливать, расстрелять (что-л.); выбивать, выбить выстрелом
separable: separable — *shoot out the tires*, *shoot the tires out*, *shoot them out*; never ✗ *shoot out them*
gloss: To destroy something by shooting at it.
examples: Kids around here *shoot out* the streetlights every summer.
The deputy *shot* the tires *out* and the truck slid to a stop.
Two windows had been *shot out* during the night.

ru: устраивать перестрелку; решать, решить исход в финальной серии
separable: the object is fixed — always *shoot it out*, never ✗ *shoot out it*; the opponent follows *with*: *shoot it out with the police*
transitivity: transitive — but only with the fixed object *it*
gloss: To settle a fight or a contest in one final exchange.
examples: The two of them *shot it out* on Main Street at noon.
The robbers had *shot it out* with police for twenty minutes before they surrendered.
If the game is still tied, they'll *shoot it out* from the penalty spot.
contrast: The noun is one word: *a shootout*. The verb stays in three: *they shot it out*.

ru: пронзать, пронзить; простреливать (о боли); проноситься, пронестись сквозь
separable: inseparable — what it passes through follows *through*: *shot through my knee*, *shot through her*; never ✗ *shot my knee through*
gloss: To pass through something suddenly and fast, especially a pain or a feeling.
examples: A sharp pain *shot through* my knee when I stood up.
Panic *shoots through* you the second the alarm goes off.
She could feel the cold *shooting through* her wet coat.
contrast: *Shot through with* is a separate, fixed use meaning 'full of, running all the way through': *a speech shot through with anger*, *marble shot through with gray*.

ru: садиться, сесть; усаживать, усадить
separable: usually no object — *sit down and eat*. With an object it splits: *sit the kids down*, *sat him down*; never ✗ *sit down him*
transitivity: both — intransitive (*please sit down*), transitive (*sat the kids down at the table*)
gloss: To lower yourself into a seated position, or to put someone else into one.
examples: Please *sit down* — the movie is about to start.
We had barely *sat down* when the power went out.
She *sat* her son *down* and asked him what had happened.
contrast: *Sit* is *sit, sat, sat*. Keep it apart from *set, set, set*: you *sit down* yourself, but you *set down* a box.

ru: садиться за стол переговоров; встречаться, встретиться для обсуждения
separable: no object — the other side follows *with*: *sit down with the union*; what you discuss follows *and*: *sit down and work it out*
gloss: To meet with someone in order to talk something through seriously.
examples: The two sides finally *sat down* last Thursday.
We need to *sit down* with our accountant before April.
They've been *sitting down* with the union every week since March.

ru: подвигаться, подвинуться (в сторону); отодвигаться, отодвинуться
separable: no object — *slide over and let me sit*; nothing comes between the two words
gloss: To move sideways along a seat or bench to make room for someone.
examples: *Slide over* — there's room for one more.
She *slid over* so he could get into the booth.
Everybody kept *sliding over* until the whole bench was full.
contrast: *Slide* keeps the same short vowel in both past forms: *slide, slid, slid* — never ✗ *slided*, and there is no ✗ *slidden*.

ru: придвигать, придвинуть; подвигать, подвинуть (по поверхности)
separable: separable — *slide over the check*, *slide the check over*, *slide it over*; never ✗ *slide over it*
gloss: To push something across a flat surface toward someone.
examples: He *slid* the envelope *over* without saying a word.
*Slide over* the salt, would you?
I've *slid* the file *over* to your side of the desk.

ru: настаивать на (своих правах); держаться за; опираться на
separable: inseparable — what you insist on follows *on*: *stand on your rights*, *stand on it*; never ✗ *stand it on*
gloss: To insist on something as a right, or to rest your case on it.
examples: He *stood on* his right to remain silent.
I'll *stand on* my record and let the voters decide.
We have never *stood on* ceremony in this house.
contrast: *Stand on ceremony* is the fixed phrase you will meet most often: *don't stand on ceremony* means 'don't be formal about it.' Forms are *stand, stood, stood*.

ru: стоять над душой; надзирать, следить за работой; контролировать
separable: inseparable — the person follows *over*: *stand over him*, *stand over the students*; never ✗ *stand him over*
gloss: To stay right next to someone and watch them while they work.
examples: I can't cook with you *standing over* me.
The nurse *stood over* him until he swallowed the pill.
He has *stood over* every batch since the recall.
contrast: One form does double duty: *stood* is both past and participle — *he stood over me*, *he has stood over me*.

ru: приклеивать, приклеить; заклеивать, заклеить; прилеплять
separable: separable — *stick down the flap*, *stick the flap down*, *stick it down*; never ✗ *stick down it*
gloss: To fasten something flat against a surface with glue or tape.
examples: *Stick* that corner *down* before somebody trips on it.
He *stuck down* the loose tile with a little glue.
The edges had been *stuck down* with masking tape.
contrast: *Stick* is *stick, stuck, stuck* — never ✗ *sticked*.

ru: вычёркивать, вычеркнуть; зачёркивать, зачеркнуть
separable: usually kept together — *strike through the wrong answer*; a pronoun can come between: *strike it through*. The passive is very common: *the clause was struck through*
gloss: To draw a line through written words to cancel them.
examples: *Strike through* anything on the form that no longer applies.
She *struck through* the last two lines and initialed the change.
The old price had been *struck through* and a lower one written above it.
contrast: *Strike* is *strike, struck, struck*. The older participle *stricken* survives only in fixed phrases — *stricken from the record*, *stricken with grief* — never ✗ *stricken through*.

ru: получать, получить (ордер) по заявлению под присягой; подавать заявление под присягой
separable: separable — *swear out a warrant*, *swear a warrant out*, *swear it out*; the object is the document, not the person, who follows *against*: *swore out a complaint against him*
gloss: To obtain a legal document such as a warrant by making a sworn statement.
examples: She *swore out* a complaint against her landlord the next morning.
A warrant had already been *sworn out* for his arrest.
As soon as the paperwork is ready, we'll *swear* it *out* at the courthouse.
contrast: *Swear* takes three different shapes: *swear, swore, sworn*. Only *sworn* can follow *have* or *be* — *a warrant was sworn out*, never ✗ *was swore out*.

ru: томиться в ожидании; мучительно ждать; переживать до конца
separable: separable — *sweat out the verdict*, *sweat the verdict out*, *sweat it out*; the form with the empty *it* is the commonest of all: *we just had to sweat it out*
gloss: To wait anxiously through something you cannot control.
examples: We *sweated out* the last two minutes of the game.
She's still *sweating out* the results of the blood test.
There's nothing to do now but *sweat* it *out*.
contrast: Unlike the other verbs in this group, *sweat* is regular in American English: *sweated out*. The bare *sweat* as a past is heard in speech, but *sweated* is what gets written. (British English prefers *sweat* for the past.)

ru: выгонять, выгнать потом (простуду); пропотеть и выздороветь; выводить с потом
separable: separable — *sweat out a cold*, *sweat the cold out*, *sweat it out*; never ✗ *sweat out it*
gloss: To get rid of an illness or a substance by sweating.
examples: He's in the sauna trying to *sweat out* a cold.
She *sweated out* the fever under three blankets.
Whatever it was, he had *sweated* it *out* by Sunday.

ru: разбрасывать, разбросать; швырять из стороны в сторону; мотать (о качке)
separable: separable — *throw the papers about*, *throw them about*, *throw about the papers*; the passive is where you hear it most: *we were thrown about the cabin*
gloss: To move or toss something violently in all directions.
examples: The storm *threw* the boat *about* for six hours.
Passengers were *thrown about* the cabin when the plane dropped.
Stop *throwing* your clothes *about* the room.
contrast: *Throw, threw, thrown* — the participle keeps its *-n*: *thrown about*, never ✗ *throwed about*. In everyday American English *throw around* is far more common than *throw about*.

ru: делать, сделать наспех; выдавать, выдать на скорую руку; строчить
separable: separable — *toss off a reply*, *toss a reply off*, *toss it off*; never ✗ *toss off it*
gloss: To produce something quickly and without much effort.
examples: He *tossed off* a two-page reply in about ten minutes.
She can *toss* a watercolor *off* between classes.
The song was *tossed off* in one afternoon and it sold a million copies.
contrast: *Toss* is regular — *tossed off* — which makes it the odd one out beside *threw*, *shot* and *stood*. In British slang *toss off* has a crude meaning, so British speakers usually pick *dash off* instead.

ru: выпивать залпом, выпить залпом; опрокидывать, опрокинуть (стакан)
separable: separable — *toss off a beer*, *toss the beer off*, *toss it off*; never ✗ *toss off it*
gloss: To drink something quickly, in one swallow.
examples: He *tossed off* the whiskey and reached for his coat.
She *tossed* the last of the coffee *off* and headed for the door.
Watch him *toss off* a shot of bourbon without blinking.
